paper_title: Leakage-aware thermal management for multi-core systems using piecewise linear model based predictive control

scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 3 and Table 1 (Section 4.1-4.2); transient comparison in Figure 4
scenario.description: Leakage-aware dynamic thermal management of a 16-core chip comparing the new piecewise-linear (PWL) model predictive control against traditional linear-model MPC, tracking an 80 C target temperature. Figure 3 gives the chip configuration, but the text gives no per-block coordinates, dimensions or powers, and no packet asset was supplied.
scenario.architecture: 16-core multi-core chip with one thermal sensor per core, configuration shown in Fig. 3 (core C32 plotted in Fig. 4)
scenario.workload: Dynamic power from Wattch running standard SPEC benchmarks, randomly assigned to different cores; golden leakage from iteration-based leakage-aware thermal simulation at 1 ms step
scenario.operating_point: Ambient 40 C, target temperature 80 C, rising range 40-80 C, falling range 120-80 C, control step 1 s, DTM activated at 1 s; Nc=1, Np=2 with 5 expansion points in Fig. 4

original_setup.solver: Golden plant: iteration-based leakage-aware thermal simulation with a 1 ms step (pdf p.5). Prediction model inside the controller: discretized RC thermal model with a piecewise-linear (Taylor-expanded) leakage model (pdf pp.2-4).
original_setup.optimizer: Closed-form unconstrained least-squares MPC solution, Pd = (V^T V + R)^-1 V^T (Yg - F T(k) - phi1 Pb - phi2 Pbn), minimizing the tracking-error cost with a power-regularization term (pdf pp.2-5).
original_setup.controller: Leakage-aware dynamic thermal management with PWL-model-based predictive control (the 'new DTM'). The scenario is Nc=1, Np=2 with 5 Taylor expansion points, a 1 s control step, an 80 C target and an ambient of 40 C. The comparator is traditional linear-model MPC with a single expansion point at 80 C (pdf pp.5-6).
original_setup.benchmark: 16-core system plant (configuration in Fig. 3, pdf p.5). Wattch dynamic power from standard SPEC benchmarks, randomly assigned to cores. Compared against traditional linear MPC in Table 1 (pdf p.6) and the C32 transient in Fig. 4 (pdf p.6).

thermal_observable.location: Per-core plant temperature, with one thermal sensor per core in the 16-core chip, tracked against the 80 C target. Fig. 4 plots core C32.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Average tracking difference between actual plant temperature and the 80 C target for the new DTM with 5 expansion points, Nc=1, Np=2 (Table 1). The maximum is 1.16 degC. The paper does not state whether the average is over cores, time, or both.

physical_mismatches.reason: The original study is a transient closed-loop DTM problem with a 1 s control step and a 1 ms plant step, using time-varying SPEC/Wattch power. A steady-state 2D solve with a one-row power trace cannot represent the controller, the predictive horizon or the transient overshoot behavior.
The controller is the main contribution (PWL MPC with Nc/Np horizons, power recommendations, DVFS and task-load adjustment). A static thermal solver has no equivalent.

The leakage-temperature feedback is nonlinear: an exponential subthreshold model, TSMC 65 nm process, PWL-approximated, with an iterated golden plant. A fixed-power thermal solve omits this coupling unless leakage is modeled separately.
The optimizer is a closed-form regularized least-squares MPC. A generic placement or thermal optimizer is not equivalent.

The paper reports a reduced-order RC network with sensor-based per-core outputs, and its package, cooling and interposer details are unspecified. The paper's temperatures (80 C target, 40 C ambient) cannot be compared numerically with any 2D Studio result.
The paper contains no 3D stack, interposer or chiplet structure and no reliability analysis beyond the falling-case range (120 to 80 C), so there is no 3D or interposer mismatch to resolve.
